name: Bilal Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a pharmacy degree, so it's chemistry, anatomy and a module called pharmacy practice where we role-play counselling a customer. Most days I'm at campus from nine to four, and I live with my uncle Tariq and his family in a flat above his phone repair shop. I work as a delivery rider for a takeaway three evenings a week, on a moped I borrow from my cousin. My parents are back in Lisbon, so I'm here on my own, more or less, and I call them on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, I never believed the big claims anyway. At the takeaway I'd say the app has been routing us for years and nothing's changed. With friends I'd say pharmacists are still the people who check what's in your medicine, so we're safe for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means the same plan: finish the degree, do the preregistration year and get registered. The concern is cost, because my parents helped with the first move but the rest is on me. My uncle doesn't charge much rent, but he expects me to help in the shop when it's busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. I'd keep the delivery shifts, which pay about ninety pounds a week on a good week, and study at the library on quiet nights. I'd ask the pharmacy at the hospital if they need a weekend assistant, since that would pay and count as experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough, but with a tight feeling about money. It's a steady kind of worry, not a frightening one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you manage deliveries and the course together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly some weeks. In December I had an anatomy exam on a Friday morning and a rush of orders the night before, so I got four hours of sleep. I learnt to ask for shifts on Mondays and Wednesdays when it's quieter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest risk to the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My moped is my cousin's, and if he sells it I've no way of working. Or if the roads freeze and there are no orders. It's small things like that, honestly, that I worry about, more than any big idea.

The delivery app has routed us for years and nothing's changed.
think: The plan is the same, but the **cost** is on me now.
My uncle charges little rent, but expects help in his shop.
do: Keep the delivery **shifts**, about ninety pounds on a good week.
Ask the hospital pharmacy about a weekend assistant job.
feel: Calm enough, with a tight **feeling** about money that is steady, not frightening.
S0.quote: My moped is my cousin's, and if he sells it I've no way of working.
fieldNote: Bilal worries about small, practical things, like a borrowed **moped**, more than any big idea about AI.
He sees the hospital pharmacy job as pay and experience together.

steps.text: Keep the Monday and Wednesday delivery shifts
Ask the hospital pharmacy about weekend assistant work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to shift things, but not wipe them out. At uni I'd ask the lecturers whether dispensing and stock checks move to machines first. With the family I'd say a pharmacist who can talk to a patient will be fine, while the ones who only count tablets might not be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think the dispensing part, the counting and labelling, is the first thing to go to software and robots. The checking of prescriptions might too. What stays is the advice, like explaining a drug to an old lady. Fewer pharmacy assistants are needed, and that's where I'd get paid work as a student.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim at the clinical side of pharmacy, like the hospital or GP surgery, where you talk to patients. I'd sign up for the clinical skills society, take the optional module on medicines for older people and practise explaining things in simple words. And I'd learn what the dispensing software does, so I'm the one who checks it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious. I can see how it could shrink the pharmacy jobs I'd have started in. But I'm steady, because the plan is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to your delivery job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The delivery job might be replaced by drones or better routing, but not soon, I think. If it goes, I'd look for a pharmacy assistant job. The trouble is those are exactly the ones that software replaces too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain this to your parents in Lisbon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm aiming at the part of the job that needs a person. My dad would say a pharmacist is a respected job, and it will always be needed. I wouldn't argue, but I'd think about what he doesn't see.

A pharmacist who talks to patients will be fine, but ones who only count tablets might not.
think: Counting and labelling go to software first, but the **advice** stays.
Fewer assistants are needed, which is where my paid work would be.
do: Aim at the **clinical** side, like hospitals or GP surgeries.
Take the medicines-for-older-people module and practise explaining in simple words.
Learn the dispensing software so I can check it.
feel: A bit **anxious** about the starter pharmacy jobs, but steady because the plan is clear.
S1.quote: What stays is the advice, like explaining a drug to an old lady.
fieldNote: Bilal splits pharmacy into **dispensing**, which is exposed, and patient advice, which he plans to focus on.
The student jobs he'd use for money are the ones that software hits first.

steps.text: Take the optional module on medicines for older people
Learn what the pharmacy dispensing software does and checks
Look for hospital pharmacy work instead of retail assistant jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too quick and someone should slow it down. I'd say it at uni and online, and I'd probably go to a meeting with other students. At home my uncle would say fix phones, nobody's robot will fix a cracked screen in two years, and that would make us laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, scared. I'd have three more years of study and I might not be able to afford even one. The pharmacy checks and dispensing would be done by AI in two years, and robots in about five. I'd worry there might be no preregistration jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the course for now. I'd ask my uncle if I can work in the repair shop full time next summer and learn phone repair, because that's hands-on and he'd teach me. I'd save every pound and ask my parents if they could keep sending a little. I'd also look at moving to a hospital pharmacy job instead of waiting for a degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's like standing at a bus stop and not knowing if the bus is coming. I'd not sleep much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes because it's only two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything's squeezed. I wouldn't finish the degree before the AI could do the checking. So I'd think about a quicker route, like becoming a pharmacy technician after the first year, which takes less time and gets me a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really go and work in your uncle's repair shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if I had to. It's not what I came for, but my uncle runs it well, and he'd teach me. I'd be embarrassed to tell my parents, but I'd do it. At least phones will still be broken in five years.

say: It's too **quick** and someone should slow it down.
My uncle says nobody's robot will fix a cracked screen in two years.
think: I'd have three more years of study and might not afford **one**.
The pharmacy checks go to AI in two years, so preregistration jobs might not exist.
do: Stay on the course for now but learn **phone repair** with my uncle next summer.
Save every pound and ask my parents to keep sending a little.
Look at becoming a pharmacy technician instead of waiting for the degree.
feel: **Alarmed**, like waiting at a bus stop without knowing if the bus is coming.
S2.quote: I'd be embarrassed to tell my parents, but I'd do it.
fieldNote: Bilal's fallback is his **uncle's** repair shop, a hands-on trade, which he would find embarrassing to tell his parents.
Two years pushes him to consider a quicker route to a wage, the pharmacy technician path.

steps.text: Look into becoming a pharmacy technician after first year
Learn phone repair in my uncle's shop next summer
Save every pound from the delivery wage
Ask my parents to keep sending a little each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to adapt, but only if you decide now. I'd tell my course friends we should look at the clinical side early. I'd tell my cousin to stop expecting the moped to last forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'd feel it's workable. I'd qualify in about 2030, which is a year or two after the thinking work goes, so I'd need to be the pharmacist who does the talking. It's uncertain, and money is still the weak point, but I'd see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying and look for the placement in a hospital pharmacy. I'd take the clinical modules and keep the delivery job on the quiet nights. I'd build savings of about eight hundred pounds. And I'd keep in contact with my uncle's shop as a plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steady. It's the kind of worry I can work with, because there's a plan and a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have in place by the time it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A registration, a hospital reference and some savings. If I can show that I helped a patient with a complex list of medicines, that would count for more than a good exam mark. I'd start by asking the placement coordinator what they look for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if your parents can't keep helping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd work more hours and take a year longer. It's not what I'd choose, but I've done it before. It'd mean the delivery job becomes the main job for a while.

say: Five years is enough to **adapt**, but only if you decide now.
I'd tell friends to look at the clinical side early.
think: I'd qualify about **2030**, so I need to be the pharmacist who does the talking.
Money is still the weak point, but I'd see a path.
do: Look for a hospital pharmacy **placement** and take the clinical modules.
Keep the delivery job on quiet nights and build savings of about eight hundred pounds.
Keep my uncle's shop as plan B.
feel: Anxious but steady, because a plan and a **date** give the worry something to work on.
S3.quote: If I can show that I helped a patient with a complex list of medicines, that would count for more than a good exam mark.
fieldNote: Bilal's plan is about **proof**: a hospital reference showing he helped a patient with complex medicines.
If his parents stop helping he would take a year longer and work more.

steps.text: Ask the placement coordinator for a hospital pharmacy placement
Save about eight hundred pounds from deliveries
Keep delivering on quiet nights and keep the repair shop as plan B

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and we should enjoy being students while we can. I'd tell my uncle his shop's safe, and he'd tell me I'm too optimistic. I'd tell my friends to get registered first, then think about other things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fairly calm. Ten years is enough to qualify, work for a few years and save. Robots would reach pharmacies when I'm about 32. The worry is whether I'd have a job at all when I'm 29, if AI does the thinking part of pharmacy before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, do my preregistration year at a hospital, and work for a few years. I'd save for my own flat. I'd learn the tools as they appear, and I'd look at a specialism like clinical pharmacy, which is hard to automate. And I'd probably bring my parents over for a visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little nervous about the unknown, but not in a way that stops me doing things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does a long warning change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be more careful with my choices. I'd not rush into a retail job just for the pay. I'd choose the route to clinical pharmacy, which is slower but safer. Ten years lets you be picky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think the next ten years would look like for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents would be retired in Lisbon. My uncle might have a second shop. I'd be in a small flat, maybe with a partner. It sounds ordinary, and that's the goal, honestly: an ordinary life that still works.

say: Ten years is long, so enjoy being **students** while we can.
Get registered first, then think about the rest.
think: I'd be fairly **calm**, because ten years is enough to qualify, work and save.
The worry is whether the thinking part of pharmacy goes before I'm 29.
do: Finish the degree, do the **preregistration** year in a hospital and save for my own flat.
Aim at clinical pharmacy, which is hard to automate.
Learn the tools as they appear.
feel: Calm, mostly, with a bit of **nervousness** about the unknown.
S4.quote: Ten years lets you be picky.
fieldNote: Bilal's long view is for a **slower**, safer route into clinical pharmacy, and he says ten years lets you be picky.
His picture of success is modest: an ordinary life that still works.

steps.text: Aim for the hospital preregistration year and clinical pharmacy
Save for a small flat of my own
Learn each new dispensing tool as the hospital brings it in

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Two years. That's the one that stops my plan before it starts. What would help is cheap fast routes into pharmacy work, like technician training, some support with rent, and honest advice from the university about what's coming.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that students who live with family, like me, are the quiet ones. We don't complain, we just do extra shifts. If things get bad, nobody will notice until we drop out.

headlineQuote: Students who live with family, like me, are the quiet ones. We don't complain, we just do extra shifts.
portrait: Bilal is a 19-year-old **pharmacy** student living with his uncle's family above a phone repair shop, far from his parents.
He is centre and steady: practical, careful with money and unwilling to take big risks.
He works as a delivery rider and worries about small things, like a borrowed moped, more than big ideas.
His plan is to aim for clinical pharmacy, with phone repair as a hands-on fallback.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most because it stops his plan before he finishes the degree.
whatWouldHelp: Fast routes into pharmacy work like **technician** training, some help with rent, and honest advice from the university.
